name: Rainbow Warrior
cardText: All conditions attractor. Doesn't imitate anything, just sparks trout attention/curiosity.
imitates: Midge and small mayfly pupae, with heavy flash
summary: A small flashy attractor nymph with a silver bead and pearl body that fish see from a long way off.
body: The Rainbow Warrior is what happens when you take a small, sober midge pupa and make it as bright as you dare. A silver bead, a body of pearl flash and a thorax of rainbow dubbing add up to a fly that catches light from every angle. On a grey winter day in slightly stained water, that visibility is exactly what gets it noticed.

It occupies a useful middle ground between imitation and attraction. It is small enough to be a plausible midge or baetis pupa, so a trout does not have to suspend disbelief entirely, but bright enough to pull fish from outside the immediate feeding lane. That combination makes it a reliable trailer behind a heavier, drabber fly.

It is especially good on tailwaters and in winter, when fish are holding deep, moving little, and need a reason to open their mouths. It also tends to work best in the first hour on a run before the fish have seen it repeatedly.
howToFish: Trail it eighteen to twenty-four inches behind a heavier nymph, dead drifted deep. Effective in Euro-nymphing rigs as the dropper.
whenToFish: Winter and early spring especially, and any time water is slightly off-colour and fish need help finding the fly.
tips: First fly through a run — its edge fades as fish see it repeatedly.
Silver bead in clear water, copper in stained.
Pairs naturally behind a Copper John or Perdigon.

name: Muddler Minnow
cardText: Don Gapen, 1930s. Invented to imitate sculpin minnows. Versatile streamer.
imitates: Sculpins, baitfish, grasshoppers and stoneflies
summary: A spun deer hair head over a turkey wing — one of the great American flies, and one that fishes as sculpin, hopper or streamer.
body: Don Gapen tied the Muddler to imitate the sculpins that big Nipigon brook trout were eating, and in doing so created a fly that has been reinterpreted more than almost any other. The broad, flat, spun deer hair head is the signature: it pushes water, it gives the fly a wide blunt profile, and it makes the whole thing behave differently from any slim streamer.

What makes it endure is its ambiguity. Fished deep and stripped, it is a sculpin. Fished dry on a greased line, it is a grasshopper — and a very good one. Fished on the swing in the surface film, it is a large emerging caddis or stonefly. Very few patterns can be fished at three depths and mean three different things.

It is genuinely difficult to tie well. Spinning and clipping deer hair to a clean profile takes practice, which is part of why fewer anglers fish it than its record deserves. It is worth the trouble, particularly for large brown trout in autumn.
howToFish: Swing it down and across like a wet fly, strip it back through likely water, or dead drift it in the film as a hopper. Weighted versions fish deep; unweighted ones can be dressed and fished dry.
whenToFish: Late summer and autumn especially, when sculpins are active and big browns are aggressive. Also excellent as a hopper substitute in August.
tips: Fish it unweighted and greased as a grasshopper — it is one of the best.
Swing it through the tail of a pool at dusk for big browns.
Trim the head flatter and wider for a more convincing sculpin profile.
materials: Head: spun and clipped deer hair with a flared collar
originNote: Tied by Don Gapen for brook trout on Ontario's Nipigon River, to imitate the sculpins the fish were feeding on.

name: Woolly Bugger
cardText: Russ Blessing's 1967 creation. Most famous streamer; imitates leeches, minnows, crayfish.
imitates: Leeches, baitfish, large nymphs and crayfish — anything alive and swimming
summary: The most versatile fly ever tied. A marabou tail, a chenille body and a palmered hackle that catches everything, everywhere.
body: If you could only take one fly anywhere in the world and fish it for anything, the argument for the Woolly Bugger is close to unanswerable. It has caught trout, bass, panfish, carp, pike, steelhead and saltwater species, in rivers, lakes and estuaries, on every continent that holds fish. That is not because it imitates one thing brilliantly — it is because it imitates the general idea of prey.

The marabou tail is the engine. Even at rest in still water, marabou breathes and pulses with the faintest current, and the palmered hackle along the body adds a second layer of movement. Underwater the fly never stops looking alive, which is a quality very few materials deliver as reliably or as cheaply.

Depending on how you fish it, it becomes different things. Stripped fast in olive it is a baitfish. Crawled slowly along the bottom in black it is a leech. Dead drifted in brown under an indicator it is a big stonefly nymph. The pattern has not changed in decades; the fisherman changes what it means.
howToFish: Cast across and down, let it swing, and strip it back in varied pulls. Also excellent dead drifted deep like a large nymph, or crawled slowly along the bottom of a lake. Vary the retrieve until something happens.
whenToFish: Every month, every water type. Particularly good in high or coloured water, at dawn and dusk, and when nothing is hatching.
tips: Black, olive and brown in #6 and #8 covers an extraordinary amount of fishing.
A cone head or bead changes it from a mid-column fly to a bottom fly.
When in doubt anywhere in the world, this is the fly.
materials: Weight: lead wire or cone head, optional
Tail: marabou, with optional Krystal Flash
Hackle: saddle hackle, palmered the length of the body

name: Soft Hackle
cardText: Sparse and elegant. Imitates emergers/soft-bodied insects.
imitates: Emerging caddis and mayflies
summary: Orange silk and a turn of partridge hackle. Two materials, three hundred years of history, and it still works.
body: The North Country soft hackles are among the oldest surviving fly patterns in the English-speaking world, and the Partridge and Orange is the most enduring of them. It is a body of orange silk and a single turn of grey partridge hackle. Nothing else. It should have been superseded a century ago and it has not been.

The reason is the hackle. Partridge fibres are soft, mottled and long, and in current they collapse and pulse around the body constantly. That movement suggests legs, gills, an emerging wing, a struggling insect — the whole impression of something alive and vulnerable in the water column, without committing to any specific insect.

It is fished on the swing, which is a technique many modern anglers have quietly abandoned in favour of indicator nymphing. That is a shame, because a team of soft hackles swung through a riffle during a caddis emergence is not just effective — it is one of the most pleasant ways to fish a river, and the takes are unmistakable.
howToFish: Cast down and across, let it swing across the current on a tight line, and hold on. Do not strike — the fish hooks itself against the swing. Fish two or three on a team for more water coverage.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn, and especially during caddis emergences and the hour before a hatch begins.
tips: Do not set the hook. Let the fish take against the tension.
Fish a team of two or three at different depths.
Orange, yellow and green silk covers most emergences.
materials: Hackle: grey partridge, one or two turns

name: Caddis Pupa
cardText: Vital stage for caddis hatches. Swing at end of drift.
imitates: Caddisflies in the pupal stage, rising to hatch
summary: The stage trout eat hardest during a caddis hatch — a pupa swimming for the surface, trailing a bubble of gas.
body: A caddis spends most of its life on the riverbed and only a few desperate minutes in open water. When it pupates it fills the space under its skin with gas, cuts loose from the bottom and rides that bubble to the surface. For those minutes it is defenceless and highly visible, and trout key on it far more heavily than they key on the adults skating around above.

That is why anglers who only fish the dry during a caddis hatch often catch less than they should. Splashy, slashing rises are usually fish taking pupae just under the film, not adults on it. The give-away is the sound: a caddis take is a slap, where a mayfly take is a sip.

The imitation leans on translucency and a suggestion of gas. A sparse, slightly shaggy body with a bright bead or an antron shuck reads as a pupa mid-ascent, and it does not need to be precise. Getting the depth and the rising motion right matters far more than the dressing.
howToFish: Fish it dead drift near the bottom, then deliberately lift and swing it through the last part of the drift so it climbs like a real pupa. That induced rise is where most takes come from.
whenToFish: Any caddis hatch from late spring through autumn, and especially in the hour before adults start appearing on the surface.
tips: If fish are slashing rather than sipping, they are on pupae, not adults.
Let it swing up at the end of every drift — do not cut the drift short.
Fish it as a dropper below an Elk Hair Caddis and cover both stages at once.
materials: Body: olive, tan or green dubbing with a fine wire rib

how to fish a caddis pupa

name: RS2
cardText: By Rim Chung. Deadly mayfly emerger for picky trout. Versatile, can be fished near surface or as a nymph.
imitates: Emerging mayflies, especially baetis, trapped in the film
summary: Rim Chung's tiny grey emerger — two materials and a wing of dubbing fluff that has humbled selective tailwater trout for decades.
body: The RS2 is about as sparse as a fly gets: a slim body, split tails and a small puff of dubbing or beaver fur for a wing. It was designed by Rim Chung in Colorado, and the name stands for Rim's Semblance 2. It looks like almost nothing in the hand, which is exactly the point.

It works because an emerging mayfly is not a crisp, well-defined insect. It is a half-shed, translucent, indistinct thing hanging in or just under the film, and hard edges are what get a fly refused on flat water. The RS2's fuzzy wing breaks up its outline the way a real emerger's does.

On tailwaters it is close to indispensable. Fished in the surface film during a baetis hatch, or a few inches down as a trailing nymph, it accounts for an enormous number of difficult fish — the ones that have already refused a well-drifted dun.
howToFish: Trail it eighteen inches behind a heavier nymph, or grease the leader and fish it in the film during a hatch. Long, fine tippet and a genuinely drag-free drift are not optional.
whenToFish: Spring and autumn baetis hatches, and through winter on tailwaters. Best when fish are visibly working but refusing dries.
tips: Grey and olive in #20 and #22 cover most situations.
When a dun gets refused, this is the next fly to try.
Tie it sparse. Bulk is what ruins it.
materials: Body: grey or olive superfine dubbing
Wing: grey beaver or muskrat fluff, short

name: WD-40
cardText: Simple Colorado pattern, deadly imitator of midges and small mayflies.
imitates: Emerging midges and small baetis mayflies
summary: A Colorado tailwater staple built from wood duck and dubbing — deadly small, deliberately plain, and hard to beat in winter.
body: The WD-40 predates the lubricant joke it gets named after; the initials stand for wood duck and dubbing, which is essentially the whole recipe. A wood duck flank tail and wingcase, a thread body and a small dubbed thorax. It takes a minute to tie and it catches fish in water where far more elaborate patterns fail.

Its usefulness comes from ambiguity at a very small size. In #20 it reads equally well as a midge pupa or an emerging baetis, and on a winter tailwater those are most of what a trout is eating. Fish that see hundreds of artificial nymphs a season rarely refuse it.
It is a fly for cold, clear, technical water. On a freestone river in July it is too subtle to be worth fishing; on a tailwater in January it is often the difference between a blank and a good day.
howToFish: Fish it deep and dead drift as the trailing fly on a two-nymph rig, or in the film during a midge emergence. Fine tippet, long leader, and patience.
whenToFish: Winter and early spring on tailwaters, and during any midge or baetis activity. A default cold-water pattern.
tips: Go smaller than feels reasonable — #20 and #22 are the working sizes.
Grey, olive and black cover almost everything.
Best as the second fly behind something heavier.
materials: Tail and wingcase: wood duck flank fibres

name: Serendipity
cardText: Craig Mathews pattern. Staple for Madison River trout and other midge-hungry trout.
imitates: Midge and caddis larvae, and emerging pupae
summary: Craig Mathews' twisted-body larva from the Madison — a scruffy deer hair head over a segmented body that trout take without hesitation.
body: The Serendipity came out of Blue Ribbon Flies in West Yellowstone and made its reputation on the Madison River. The body is twisted Z-lon or antron, which gives a tight, translucent segmentation that looks convincingly like a midge or small caddis larva, and the clipped deer hair head gives it a blunt profile and a little buoyancy.

It is one of those patterns that works better than its simplicity suggests. Midge larvae are among the most abundant trout foods in any river, available every month of the year, and a fly that reads as a segmented worm-like larva rarely gets examined closely.

Red, olive and brown are the standard colours. Red is worth carrying specifically: in slightly coloured water or low light it is noticeably easier for a fish to find, and it is a well-known confidence colour on the Madison and elsewhere.
howToFish: Dead drift deep under an indicator, usually as the trailing fly. It also fishes well swung up at the end of the drift during an emergence.
whenToFish: Year round, and particularly productive in autumn and winter when midge larvae make up most of a trout's diet.
tips: Red is not a gimmick here — carry it.
Excellent trailing fly behind a heavier stonefly nymph.
Keep the deer hair head small; a bulky head kills the profile.
materials: Body: twisted Z-lon or antron in red, olive or brown

name: Snow Cone Midge
cardText: White bead imitates gas bubble. Excellent lake pattern.
imitates: Chironomid pupae hanging in the water column
summary: A chironomid pupa with a white bead head that reads as the gas bubble of an insect about to hatch. A stillwater specialist.
body: Chironomids are the single most important food source in most trout lakes, and the pupa is the stage that matters. It hangs almost motionless in the water column, slowly rising, and trout patrol specific depth bands intercepting them by the hundred.

The white bead is doing precise imitative work rather than adding flash. As a chironomid pupa prepares to emerge, gas collects under the skin at the thorax and shows as a distinct pale, glassy bubble at the head. A white or pearl bead is a remarkably good copy of it, and on hard-fished lakes the difference between a white bead and a gold one can be dramatic.
This is a fly that demands discipline rather than skill. It is fished static, at a measured depth, for long periods. Anglers who cannot resist retrieving it catch very little.
howToFish: Suspend it under an indicator at a measured depth, typically within a foot or two of the bottom, and leave it alone. Let the wind provide any movement.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn on lakes and ponds, with the heaviest chironomid activity in late spring and early summer.
tips: Do not retrieve. The natural barely moves.
Depth is everything — adjust in one-foot increments until you find the band.
Black and red bodies with a white bead cover most lakes.
materials: Hook: curved nymph or buzzer hook, #12-#16
Body: black, red or olive thread, wire ribbed

name: Disco Midge
cardText: Flashy midge larva/emerger; deadly in tailwaters in winter.
imitates: Midge larvae and pupae, with deliberate flash
summary: A flashy tinsel-bodied midge for cold tailwater winters, when fish need help finding a very small fly.
body: The Disco Midge is a midge pattern that abandons subtlety. The body is pearl or coloured tinsel over a bare hook, so it catches and throws light from every angle, and at #20 that flash is often the only reason a trout notices it at all.

That makes it a specialist for particular conditions: cold water, low light, slightly stained flows, and deep runs where visibility is the limiting factor rather than selectivity. In gin-clear flat water it can be too much, and a plain Zebra Midge will usually outfish it.

It is a winter tailwater fly above all. When fish are stacked deep and barely moving, a small bright object drifting past at the right depth gets eaten by fish that will not move six inches for anything drab.
howToFish: Dead drift deep on a long leader under an indicator, as the trailing fly behind something heavier. Get it right down to the fish.
whenToFish: Winter and early spring on tailwaters, and any time water is off-colour and fish need help finding the fly.
tips: Best in the first drifts through a run, before fish have seen it repeatedly.
Pearl and red are the two to carry.
If the water is very clear and flat, switch to a plainer midge.
materials: Bead: silver or black tungsten, optional
Body: pearl or coloured Mylar tinsel

how to fish a disco midge

name: Zebra Midge
cardText: Most effective in cold tailwaters when no dries are visible. Classic go-to midge pattern.
imitates: Midge pupae
summary: Thread, wire and a bead. The simplest fly in the box and the one that saves winter tailwater days.
body: A Zebra Midge is a bead, a thread body and a wire rib. That is the entire fly. It takes ninety seconds to tie and it is, on many tailwaters, the single most productive pattern in the box for eight months of the year.

Midge pupae are the most consistently available trout food in cold water. They are present in enormous numbers, they are active every month including January, and they are small, dark and slim — which is precisely what a thread body with a wire rib looks like. The bead adds the flash of a gas bubble forming under the pupal skin as the insect prepares to rise.

The discipline it demands is going small enough. Anglers routinely fish a #18 when the fish are eating a #22. On a pressured tailwater in winter, dropping two sizes and lengthening the tippet solves more problems than any other adjustment.
howToFish: Dead drift deep on a long leader under an indicator, usually as the trailing fly behind something heavier. On stillwaters, fish it static under a bobber and let the fish hook themselves.
whenToFish: All year, and essential in winter. Tailwaters in particular fish midges almost every day of the season.
tips: Black with a silver bead and red with a copper bead cover most water.
Go smaller than feels sensible. #20 and #22 are not extreme.
The trailing fly in a two-nymph rig is where this pattern belongs.
materials: Hook: curved scud or standard nymph, #16-#24
Bead: silver, copper or black tungsten
Body: black, red or olive thread
Rib: fine silver or copper wire

name: Green Weenie
cardText: Bright chartreuse chenille. Deadly simple attractor for stocked and recently planted trout.
imitates: Inchworms and caddis larvae
summary: A loop of bright green chenille. Absurdly simple, faintly ridiculous, and deadly on Appalachian streams.
body: The Green Weenie is a loop of chartreuse chenille on a hook, sometimes with a bead. It is one of the simplest flies anyone fishes, it looks like nothing an entomologist would recognise, and on eastern and Appalachian streams it catches trout with a consistency that irritates people who prefer their flies dignified.

The most likely explanation is inchworms. Green caterpillars drop out of streamside trees in enormous numbers in late spring and early summer, and a bright green tube is a decent representation of one. It also passes for a caddis larva, and in the smaller sizes for a variety of green grubs that end up in the drift.

It is worth carrying for exactly the days when nothing else is working. On a bright, low, clear stream in June where every trout has refused three respectable patterns, a Green Weenie under an indicator will often produce the first fish of the afternoon.
howToFish: Dead drift under an indicator or as a dropper below a dry fly. Fish it close to overhanging trees and brush where real inchworms would be falling in.
whenToFish: Late spring and early summer, when inchworms are dropping from streamside vegetation. Effective through summer on freestone streams.
tips: Fish it tight under overhanging trees — that is where the naturals fall.
A superb dropper beneath a dry fly on small streams.
Do not let its appearance put you off. It works.
materials: Body: chartreuse chenille, tied as a loop or short tag

name: Lightning Bug
cardText: Flashy beadhead, imitates mayflies. Great in off-colored water.
imitates: Small mayfly nymphs, with heavy attractor flash
summary: A tinsel-bodied beadhead that shines through stained water. Half imitation, half attention-grabber, and consistently effective.
body: The Lightning Bug is built around flash. A pearl or silver tinsel body, a wire rib and a bright bead give it more reflectivity than almost any other small nymph, while the overall shape stays convincingly mayfly-like. It is an attractor that has not given up on imitation.

That balance is what makes it useful. A fly that is purely flashy gets refused by educated fish; a fly that is purely imitative can go unnoticed in coloured or fast water. The Lightning Bug sits between the two, which is why it works in the conditions that defeat both.
It comes into its own after rain, during spring runoff, and in the low light at either end of the day. In clear, flat, heavily pressured water it is usually the wrong choice.
howToFish: Dead drift deep under an indicator or in a Euro-nymph rig. Very effective as the lead fly with a drabber nymph trailing behind it.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn, particularly in off-coloured or high water and in low light.
tips: Pair it as the attractor ahead of something natural — the flash pulls fish, the second fly gets eaten.
Pearl is the standard; try chartreuse in muddy water.
Lose confidence in it on clear flat water. That is the right instinct.

how to fish a lightning bug

name: Clouser Minnow
cardText: Bob Clouser, 1987. Effective for bass, trout, and saltwater species.
imitates: Baitfish and minnows
summary: Dumbbell eyes and bucktail. It swims hook-point-up with a jigging motion and has probably caught more species than any other fly.
body: The Clouser Minnow is built around one mechanical idea: put heavy dumbbell eyes on top of the hook shank, and the fly will flip over and ride point-up. That single decision does two things. It makes the fly almost snag-proof over rock and weed, and it gives it a pronounced jigging action on the retrieve — rising and diving with every strip rather than swimming flat.

That darting, wounded motion is what predatory fish respond to. A healthy baitfish swims steadily; an injured one falls and recovers, falls and recovers. The Clouser does the latter automatically, without the angler having to do anything clever.

Bob Clouser designed it for Susquehanna smallmouth, but it has since been used to catch a genuinely absurd range of species in fresh and salt water. Chartreuse over white is the classic, and remains the first choice almost everywhere; olive over white is the better trout colour on most rivers.
howToFish: Cast across and strip back in sharp pulls with pauses. The pause is where the take usually comes — the fly is dropping and looks wounded. Vary strip length and speed until you find the pattern.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn wherever fish are eating baitfish. Prime time is any period of low light or high aggression.
tips: The take almost always comes on the pause. Do not strip continuously.
Chartreuse/white for bass and salt, olive/white for trout.
It rides hook-up — fish it confidently over rock and structure.
materials: Eyes: lead or brass dumbbell, tied on top of the shank
originNote: Developed by Bob Clouser for smallmouth bass on the Susquehanna River, and since credited with more species caught than nearly any other fly.

name: Duracell Nymph
cardText: Jig-style with UV brown body (purple sheen); versatile attractor/mayfly imitator.
imitates: Mayfly nymphs, with a UV-active attractor sheen
summary: A jig nymph with a coppery-purple UV body — a modern competition pattern that fish take as both food and curiosity.
body: The Duracell takes its name from the battery, because the body has the same coppery-bronze look with a purple sheen shifting through it. The effect comes from UV-active dubbing, and under water it produces a colour that is genuinely difficult to describe and apparently very difficult for trout to ignore.

Structurally it is a modern competition nymph: a jig hook, a slotted tungsten bead, a slim tapered body and a soft hackle collar. The jig hook rides point-up, so it snags far less on the bottom, which matters when the whole technique depends on fishing within an inch of the riverbed.

It sits in the same family as the Frenchie and the Perdigon and is fished the same way. Where it differs is colour: on days when hot-spot pink has been shown to every fish in the run, the Duracell's more muted, ambiguous shimmer often keeps producing.
howToFish: Built for tight-line and Euro-nymphing: short upstream casts, rod tip leading the fly, constant contact, no indicator. Also works as the point fly in a conventional rig.
whenToFish: Year round. Especially useful on pressured water where fish have learned the more obvious hot-spot patterns.
tips: Fish it as the anchor with a lighter nymph on a dropper above.
Slotted tungsten on a jig hook — the point-up ride is half the value.
A good rotation fly when a Frenchie stops producing.
materials: Body: UV-active bronze/purple dubbing, wire ribbed
Collar: soft hackle or hot spot dubbing
searchTerms: what does a duracell nymph imitate
how to fish a duracell nymph

name: Blowtorch
cardText: Attractor with hot spot tag; peacock body triggers strikes.
imitates: Mayfly and small stonefly nymphs, with a hot collar
summary: A peacock-bodied jig nymph with a blaze orange collar and rubber legs — a competition attractor that fishes far bigger than its size.
body: The Blowtorch was designed by Devin Olsen out of competition fishing, and it is an unusually well-judged combination of triggers. A peacock herl body gives natural iridescence, a fluorescent orange collar gives a point of focus, and two short rubber legs add movement that most Euro-nymphs deliberately lack.

Those legs are the interesting choice. Competition nymphs generally strip away anything that slows the sink rate, but a small amount of leg movement makes the fly read as alive in a way a bare resin body does not. It is a deliberate trade of a little sink speed for a lot of animation.

It fishes as a general attractor nymph rather than an imitation of anything specific, which makes it an excellent searching fly on water you do not know. Where a Perdigon is a scalpel, the Blowtorch is a fly you tie on to find out where the fish are.
howToFish: Tight-line or indicator nymphing, dead drift close to the bottom. Effective as either the anchor or the dropper depending on bead weight.
whenToFish: Year round, and a strong first choice when prospecting unfamiliar water.
tips: The orange collar is the trigger — do not tie it sparse.
Excellent searching fly when you have no information about a river.
Pair it with a drabber nymph so you cover both approaches at once.
materials: Collar: fluorescent orange thread or dubbing

name: Frenchie
cardText: Pheasant tail variant; slim profile, hot spot collar.
imitates: Mayfly nymphs with a bright hot spot
summary: A Pheasant Tail with a hot pink collar — the small change that made an old fly a competition staple.
body: The Frenchie is a Pheasant Tail nymph with the thorax replaced by a band of bright pink or orange dubbing. That is the entire modification, and it is enough to have made it one of the most widely fished nymphs in competition and guide circles.

The hot spot works by giving the trout a specific point to focus on. In moving water, a fish has a fraction of a second to locate and intercept a small object, and a concentrated flash of contrasting colour makes that easier. The rest of the fly stays sober and imitative, so it does not tip over into looking artificial.

It fishes exactly like a Pheasant Tail but tends to outperform it in faster, deeper, or slightly coloured water where visibility is the limiting factor. On clear, slow, heavily pressured water the plain version is often still the better choice — carry both and let the water decide.
howToFish: Dead drift deep, tight-line or under an indicator. Excellent as the dropper behind a heavier anchor fly.
whenToFish: Year round. Particularly effective in faster or slightly stained water, and during baetis activity in spring and autumn.
tips: Pink is the classic hot spot; orange and chartreuse both have their days.
Carry a plain Pheasant Tail alongside for clear, pressured water.
A jig hook and slotted tungsten bead makes it far more snag-resistant.
materials: Body: pheasant tail fibres, wire ribbed
Thorax: hot pink or orange dubbing

name: Perdigon
cardText: Spanish fly. Slim, sinks fast. 'Perdigon' = pellet/shot (as in ammo). Many color patterns to imitate different insects.
imitates: Mayfly nymphs, fished as a fast-sinking competition pattern
summary: A slim, resin-coated Euro-nymph built for one purpose: getting to the bottom faster than anything else in the box.
body: The Perdigon came out of European competition fishing, where getting a fly to the correct depth in the shortest possible distance is the entire game. The body is thread and tinsel coated in UV resin, which makes it hard, smooth and completely non-absorbent. Water slides off it rather than dragging on it, and with a tungsten bead it drops through a run like a stone.

That sink rate changes what is possible. In a fast, deep pocket where a conventional dubbed nymph would still be in the upper third of the water column by the time it left the seam, a Perdigon is on the bottom in the first metre. It puts the fly in front of fish that most anglers never reach.

The hot spot — a band of bright thread behind the bead — is doing real work. In broken water it gives a trout a point of focus, and in competition testing the difference between a hot-spotted and plain version is consistent enough that almost nobody ties them plain any more.
howToFish: Built for tight-line and Euro-nymphing: short casts upstream, rod tip leading the fly, contact maintained throughout, no indicator. Also works well as the anchor in a conventional indicator rig.
whenToFish: Year round, and particularly valuable in fast, deep water and in cold months when fish hold hard on the bottom.
tips: Tungsten, not brass. The whole point is sink rate.
A hot spot in orange, pink or chartreuse consistently outfishes a plain body.
Keep the profile slim — bulk defeats the purpose of the fly.
materials: Body: thread with tinsel rib, coated in UV resin
Hot spot: fluorescent thread collar behind the bead

name: Hare's Ear Nymph
cardText: Versatile nymph, imitates many aquatic insects. Confidence fly.
imitates: Mayfly nymphs, caddis pupae and scuds — deliberately ambiguous
summary: A scruffy bundle of hare's mask fur that suggests half a dozen insects at once and has never gone out of style.
body: Where the Pheasant Tail is slim and precise, the Hare's Ear is deliberately messy. It is dubbed from the mask of a hare, guard hairs and all, and the whole point is that the guard hairs stick out at every angle. Underwater those fibres move constantly, and that suggestion of legs and gills and general life is worth more than any anatomical accuracy.

Its ambiguity is a feature. Depending on size and how you fish it, the same fly reads as a mayfly nymph, a caddis pupa, a scud, a sowbug, or a small stonefly. On unfamiliar water where you have no idea what the fish are eating, a Hare's Ear is a reasonable first guess and a hard fly to be badly wrong with.

It is at its very best during caddis emergences, fished with a swing at the end of the drift. The buggy silhouette rising through the water column is close enough to a pupa struggling toward the surface that fish commit hard. Old, simple and still one of the best nymphs in any box.
howToFish: Dead drift under an indicator, or as a dropper below a dry. Deliberately swing it up at the end of the drift during caddis activity. Do not be afraid to let it tumble along the bottom.
whenToFish: Year round. Particularly good in spring and during caddis emergences, and as a searching nymph on water you do not know.
tips: Pick out the dubbing with a needle after tying — scruffier fishes better.
Carry it beaded and unbeaded; they fish like two different flies.
A superb dropper behind an Elk Hair Caddis in summer.
materials: Body: hare's mask dubbing, picked out
Rib: fine gold tinsel or wire
Wing case: turkey or pheasant tail

name: Pheasant Tail Nymph
cardText: Frank Sawyer's design, imitates mayflies. A staple in U.S. waters.
imitates: Mayfly nymphs, especially baetis
summary: The most effective mayfly nymph ever tied — a slim bundle of pheasant fibres that has been catching trout for seventy years.
body: Frank Sawyer built this fly out of two materials because that was all he thought it needed: pheasant tail fibres for the body and fine copper wire to bind them and add weight. There is no thread in the original dressing. Seventy years later it remains the first nymph most anglers tie on and the last one they give up on.

It works because mayfly nymphs are slim, tapered, brown and translucent, and pheasant tail fibres are all four of those things at once. The colour shifts subtly as it wets, the fibre tips make convincing tails and legs, and the wire gives it just enough weight to get down without the fly looking like a piece of hardware. Nothing about it is loud.

Its range is remarkable. In #18 and smaller it is a baetis nymph on a winter tailwater; in #12 it is a larger mayfly nymph on a spring freestone. Beadhead versions get it deeper faster; the original unweighted version fishes beautifully in the film during an emergence. If you had to fish one nymph for the rest of your life, the argument for this one is difficult to beat.
howToFish: Dead drift under an indicator or as the point fly in a two-nymph rig. Also deadly fished as a dropper below a dry. At the end of the drift let it swing and rise — the lift imitates an emerging nymph and draws savage takes.
whenToFish: Every month of the year. Strongest before and during mayfly hatches, when nymphs are active and moving toward the surface.
tips: The unweighted original is a superb emerger; do not assume you always want a bead.
Size down before you change patterns — #18 solves more problems than a new fly.
Let it swing at the end of every drift. That is where a third of the takes come from.
materials: Weight: copper wire underbody, optional bead
Body: pheasant tail fibres wound and ribbed with copper wire
Thorax: peacock herl or built-up copper wire
Wing case: pheasant tail fibres pulled over
originNote: Devised by Frank Sawyer, a river keeper on the Wiltshire Avon, using only pheasant tail fibres and copper wire — no thread at all.

name: Prince Nymph
cardText: By Doug Prince, 1930s. White wings, peacock body. Excellent attractor.
imitates: Stonefly and mayfly nymphs, with attractor flash
summary: Peacock herl and two white biot wings — an old attractor nymph that keeps outfishing more accurate patterns.
body: The Prince Nymph should not work as well as it does. Real nymphs do not have two bright white wings folded over their backs. But peacock herl has an iridescence that no synthetic has ever quite matched, and those white biots give a fish something specific to aim at in murky, broken, fast-moving water.

It is best understood as an attractor that happens to be nymph-shaped. Fished in pocket water and riffles where trout decide quickly, it gets eaten by fish that are not examining anything closely. On flat, clear, heavily fished water it is far less convincing, and there are better choices.

In the larger sizes it makes a credible stonefly nymph, which is why it is so productive on western freestone rivers in spring and early summer. Fish it big and deep in high water, and small as a dropper in summer.
howToFish: Dead drift deep under an indicator, or as the lead fly ahead of a smaller natural nymph. Also very good on the swing at the end of a drift.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn, particularly in fast or slightly coloured water and during stonefly activity.
tips: Go bigger than you think in spring high water — #10 and #12 earn their place.
The white biots are the trigger; if they are chewed off, change the fly.
Pairs beautifully as the lead fly ahead of a Pheasant Tail.
materials: Wings: white goose biots, tied flat over the back

name: Copper John
cardText: By John Barr, 1990s. Weighted with copper wire, gets down quickly. Good mayfly/stonefly imitator.
imitates: Mayfly and stonefly nymphs, with an attractor's flash
summary: A wire-bodied nymph built to sink fast and flash hard — as much an anchor as an imitation.
body: John Barr designed the Copper John to solve a practical problem: getting a nymph rig to the bottom quickly in fast water. A body of wound copper wire, a tungsten or brass bead, and a lacquered wing case make it one of the densest nymphs you can fish, and it drags a lighter trailing fly down with it.

But it is not merely ballast. The wire body has a hard, segmented, translucent look that reads convincingly as a mayfly or small stonefly nymph, and the flash of copper in moving water is a genuine trigger. Trout in fast riffles have very little time to decide, and a bright, dense, buggy object tumbling past gets eaten.

It comes in a dozen wire colours and most of them catch fish. Copper is the original and still the most reliable; red and chartreuse have their days, particularly in off-coloured water. As the lead fly in a two-nymph rig with something softer behind it, this is one of the most productive setups in western fly fishing.
howToFish: Fish it as the heavy point fly in a two-nymph rig, or as the anchor in Euro-nymphing. Dead drift close to the bottom — if you are not occasionally ticking rocks, you are not deep enough.
whenToFish: Spring through autumn in fast, broken water. Especially useful in high or coloured water when you need weight and visibility.
tips: Use it as the anchor and hang a soft, natural nymph eighteen inches behind.
Red is worth carrying for off-coloured spring flows.
Tungsten bead versions sink noticeably faster and are worth the extra cost.
materials: Wing case: black Thin Skin over flash, epoxied
originNote: Designed by John Barr in Colorado as a heavy point fly that would sink a nymph rig fast.

name: Pat's Rubber Legs
cardText: Also called Girdle Bug. Popular Western stonefly imitation.
imitates: Stonefly nymphs
summary: Chenille and rubber legs. It looks like nothing much in the hand and like a stonefly nymph in the water.
body: Stonefly nymphs live in freestone rivers for up to three years before emerging, which means there is a substantial population of large, meaty nymphs available to trout every single day of the year. That is an unusual thing in fly fishing: a big food item that is never out of season.

Pat's Rubber Legs is the simplest credible imitation of one. A chenille body, a set of rubber legs at each end and a bead or lead underbody to sink it. In the hand it looks crude. In the water the rubber legs undulate constantly with the current, and that movement is the whole fly — it is the difference between a piece of chenille and something a trout believes is alive.

It is most valuable as the heavy fly in a two-nymph rig on a big freestone river. Fish it deep and slow through the runs and along the drop-offs. In spring high water, when everything is brown and pushing, this is frequently the fly that keeps working when nothing subtle will.
howToFish: Deep and slow. Fish it as the anchor fly under an indicator with a smaller nymph trailing behind, and get it genuinely on the bottom. Do not strip it — dead drift is what stoneflies do.
whenToFish: All year on freestone rivers, and outstanding in spring high water and during the pre-emergence period before a stonefly hatch.
tips: Coffee/black and brown/tan are the two colours worth carrying.
If you are not losing the occasional fly to the bottom, you are fishing too shallow.
The bigger sizes are not a gimmick — #6 and #8 catch large fish.
materials: Weight: lead wire underbody or tungsten bead
Legs: round rubber legs at tail, thorax and head

name: Balanced Leech
cardText: Hangs horizontal under indicator; deadly stillwater/leech imitation.
imitates: Leeches suspended horizontally in the water column
summary: A leech tied on an extended pin so it hangs perfectly level under an indicator instead of nose-down.
body: A conventional weighted fly suspended under an indicator hangs nose-down, which looks nothing like a leech. The balanced pattern solves this by mounting a bead on a pin extending forward from the hook eye, moving the centre of gravity ahead of the hook so the fly hangs horizontally — exactly the posture a leech holds when it stops swimming.

It matters more than it sounds. Stillwater trout cruising a shoreline see a suspended fly for several seconds before deciding, and posture is one of the few cues available when the fly is not moving. A level leech reads as the real animal; a vertical one reads as a jig.

Fished under an indicator over a drop-off or weed edge, it is one of the most effective stillwater techniques there is, and it works in cold water when trout will not chase a stripped fly. In winter and early spring on a lake it is frequently the difference between fish and no fish.
howToFish: Suspend under an indicator at a measured depth over drop-offs and weed edges. Let wind drift and small twitches provide the movement — do not retrieve steadily.
whenToFish: Year round on stillwaters, and especially valuable in cold water when trout will not chase.
tips: Black, maroon and olive are the colours that matter.
Set the depth so the fly sits just above the weed or bottom.
A tiny twitch every twenty seconds is often all the movement needed.
materials: Pin: straight pin extending from the hook eye with a tungsten bead
Body: dubbing or chenille with a wire rib

name: Deer Hair Mouse
cardText: Big trout and bass love it. Exciting topwater strikes.
imitates: Mice and voles swimming across the surface at night
summary: A spun deer hair mouse fished after dark for the largest brown trout in the river. Few takes, and none of them quiet.
body: Big brown trout are not primarily insect feeders. Past a certain size the arithmetic stops working, and they shift to hunting whatever large, warm and careless thing enters the water — which, on a summer night, regularly includes mice and voles swimming a river they misjudged.

Mousing is a genuinely different discipline from the rest of fly fishing. It happens in the dark, the fly is large and air-resistant, and the presentation is a steady swimming wake rather than a drag-free drift. You are not matching a hatch; you are imitating an animal in trouble.

Expect very few takes and remember that a big trout often drowns a mouse before eating it. The classic mistake is striking at the splash. Wait until you feel the weight of the fish on the line, then set.
howToFish: Cast across and slightly down, and swim it with a steady retrieve so it pushes a visible V-wake. Fish it tight to banks and undercuts. Do not set on the splash — set when you feel weight.
whenToFish: Warm summer nights, from full dark onward. Overcast, moonless nights are traditionally best.
tips: Set on feel, not on sound. This is the single most important thing.
Heavy tippet — 0X or 1X. The takes are violent and the fish are large.
Fish water you have already scouted in daylight.
materials: Body: spun and clipped deer hair

name: Parachute Adams
cardText: Mayfly variation with parachute hackle, floats lower, easier to see.
imitates: Mayfly duns and emergers sitting in the surface film
summary: The Adams rebuilt to sit low in the film, with a white post you can actually see. Probably the most-fished dry fly in America.
body: The parachute variant takes everything that works about the Adams and fixes its one real weakness. Instead of standing on a collar of hackle wound around the hook shank, the fly hangs its body in the surface film with the hackle wound horizontally around an upright post. The result looks, from below, far more like an insect that has just struggled out of its shuck and is lying flat and vulnerable on the water.

That lower profile matters most when fish are being selective, which is to say on flat water, in slow currents, and late in a hatch when the easy fish have already been caught. A standard hackled dry perched high on its tiptoes is a convincing mayfly on broken water and a suspicious one on a glassy pool. The parachute is the version that keeps working after the water goes quiet.

The white or bright post is not for the fish — it is for you. Being able to track a #20 fly at thirty feet in low light is the difference between a hooked trout and a rise you noticed a second too late. This one practical detail is why the pattern has quietly become the default dry fly in most American fly boxes.
howToFish: Fish it exactly like a standard dry — drag-free dead drift — but do not be afraid to let it swing at the very end. A parachute dragging under at the end of the drift is a passable emerger and gets eaten more often than it should.
whenToFish: Any mayfly hatch, and particularly on flat or slow water where a high-riding fly gets refused. Excellent in the last hour of light when you cannot see a dark fly.
tips: Use a bright orange or pink post in flat light and a white one against dark water.
In #20 and smaller, this fly covers most baetis and midge situations by itself.
If it starts sinking, do not dress it with floatant — change to a dry fly and let the old one dry in your patch.
materials: Tail: mixed grizzly and brown hackle fibres
Post: white calf body hair or synthetic yarn
Hackle: grizzly, wound parachute-style around the post

name: Salmonfly
cardText: Giant stonefly imitation; deadly during Western salmonfly hatches.
imitates: Adult giant stoneflies of the genus Pteronarcys
summary: The biggest dry fly hatch in the West. For two weeks a year, trout abandon caution for a three-inch insect.
body: Salmonflies are enormous — a mature adult is a genuinely large insect, orange-bodied and clumsy — and their emergence on western freestone rivers is the most anticipated event of the fly fishing calendar. Nymphs crawl to the banks to hatch, adults clamber in the streamside willows, and the ones that fall in do not go unnoticed.

The hatch moves upstream as water temperatures climb, often several miles a day, which means timing is everything and a river can be red hot one morning and finished the next. Local knowledge, or a phone call to a fly shop, is worth more than any pattern choice.

Because the naturals are so large, presentation forgiveness is unusually high. A salmonfly imitation can land hard, drag a little and still get eaten. What it must do is float — a waterlogged fly this size is useless — and be visible enough for you to track in heavy water.
howToFish: Fish it tight to the banks and the willows, where the adults actually fall in. Let it land audibly. Twitching it occasionally imitates a struggling adult and often triggers the take.
whenToFish: Late spring and early summer on western freestone rivers, as the hatch works its way upstream. A narrow window, typically two to three weeks on any given stretch.
tips: Call a local fly shop. The hatch moves miles a day and timing beats pattern.
Fish the bank. The insects come from the willows, not midstream.
Carry a nymph too — the days before the adults appear can be better than the hatch itself.

name: Yellow Sally
cardText: Imitates Little Yellow Sally stoneflies; great summer hatch-matcher.
imitates: Adult little yellow stoneflies
summary: The small yellow stonefly of high summer — an easy hatch to miss, and a very easy one to fish once you see it.
body: Little Yellow Sallies are small, bright yellow stoneflies that come off through summer on freestone rivers, usually in the afternoon and evening. They are far less dramatic than the salmonfly hatch and get correspondingly less attention, which is part of why they are so useful: the fish see plenty of them and the anglers often do not.

The distinguishing feature is colour. A Yellow Sally is a clean, slightly luminous pale yellow, sometimes with a small orange or red egg sac at the rear of the female. That egg sac is a real trigger, and imitations that include it tend to outfish ones that do not.

They are also poor fliers and frequently end up on the water, which means a Yellow Sally imitation works as a searching dry through summer even when no hatch is obvious. If you see small yellow insects fluttering near the bank, tie one on.
howToFish: Dead drift along banks, seams and riffle edges. An occasional twitch imitates the adult's clumsy fluttering and draws attention.
whenToFish: Summer afternoons and evenings on freestone rivers, roughly June through August.
tips: Include the small orange or red egg sac — it matters.
Watch the willows and the bank grass; if there are small yellow insects there, fish it.
A good searching dry even with no visible hatch.
materials: Body: pale yellow dubbing with an orange butt
Wing: light elk or deer hair

name: Grasshopper
cardText: Classic late-summer terrestrial. Big meal that draws aggressive rises from trout.
imitates: Adult grasshoppers
summary: The classic deer hair grasshopper — a mouthful of protein that brings the biggest fish in the run to the surface.
body: By late summer the grass along a trout river is full of hoppers, and a meaningful number of them end up in the water every windy afternoon. A grasshopper is an enormous meal compared to a mayfly, and trout that have spent all season sipping tiny insects will abandon a feeding lane entirely to intercept one.

Dave Whitlock's pattern is the standard against which hopper flies are still measured. The spun and clipped deer hair head gives it a convincing blunt profile, the knotted legs suggest the real insect's distinctive kick, and the turkey wing lies over the body the way a hopper's does. It looks like the animal in a way that foam patterns, for all their practicality, do not quite manage.

Hopper fishing is fundamentally about the bank. The insects come from land, so the fish that eat them hold tight to the edges — under grass, against undercuts, in the eighteen inches of water closest to shore. Fishing the middle of the river with a hopper is mostly wasted effort.
howToFish: Cast tight to grassy banks and let it land hard. Dead drift along the edge, with an occasional twitch. Takes are often violent; wait until the fish has turned down before setting.
whenToFish: Late July through September, best on hot, windy afternoons when hoppers are getting blown into the water.
tips: Wind is your friend. The windier the afternoon, the better hopper fishing gets.
Fish it within a foot of the bank, then closer.
Pause after the take — hopper eats are slow and deliberate more often than not.
materials: Body: yellow poly yarn or dubbing with a red tail tuft
Head: spun and clipped deer hair

name: Ant
cardText: Simple but deadly terrestrial. Trout key on ants that fall or blow onto the water.
imitates: Winged ants during a mating flight
summary: When a flying ant fall happens, trout eat nothing else. A two-lump body and a flat wing is all it takes.
body: Ant falls are the closest thing in fly fishing to a lottery win. Winged ants swarm for mating flights on specific warm, still afternoons, usually in late summer, and when the swarm drifts over water thousands of them land and cannot get off. Every trout in the river feeds, often recklessly, and they will refuse anything that is not an ant.

The imitation is almost comically simple: two distinct lumps separated by a pinched waist, and a flat wing lying over the back. That waist is the single most important feature. It is the silhouette a trout uses to identify an ant, and a fly without a clear pinch between the segments gets refused during a serious fall.

Ants are also worth fishing when nothing is happening at all. Wingless ants fall into streams all summer, and a small black ant fished dead drift under overhanging trees is one of the more reliable ways to move a fish on a slow, hot afternoon.
howToFish: Dead drift on fine tippet. The fly rides flush and low, so track it by the leader or fish it as a dropper behind a visible dry. Takes are quiet sips.
whenToFish: Late summer and early autumn on warm, humid, windless afternoons — the classic conditions for a mating flight. Wingless versions work all summer.
tips: If you see fish feeding steadily on nothing visible in August, suspect ants.
Keep the waist pinched and distinct. It is the trigger.
Carry black and cinnamon in #16 and #18.
materials: Body: two black dubbing or foam segments with a pinched waist
Wing: white poly yarn or hackle tips, tied flat over the back
Hackle: black, sparse, at the waist

name: Beetle
cardText: High-floating foam beetle. The distinctive “plop” often triggers immediate strikes.
imitates: Terrestrial beetles
summary: A small black slab that sits flush in the film — the most underrated terrestrial there is.
body: Beetles are the most abundant terrestrial insect on earth and they fall into trout streams constantly, yet most anglers reach for a hopper first. That is a mistake. A beetle imitation catches fish through the whole summer, on water where a hopper would be too much fly, and it does so with no hatch, no timing and no entomology required.

The critical detail is how it sits. A real beetle is dense and does not float high — it lies flush in the surface film, half in and half out, showing a solid black oval from below. A properly tied foam beetle does the same. If your beetle is riding up on hackle points, it is the wrong shape entirely.

It is also a superb fly for shaded small streams and for spooky fish in slow, clear water. It lands quietly, it looks like an accident, and it does not demand a drag-free drift the way a mayfly imitation does. Fish that have refused three dries will often eat a beetle without hesitation.
howToFish: Cast under overhanging trees, along shaded banks, and to fish holding in slow clear water. Dead drift. Because it sits flush it is hard to see — use a small bright indicator post or fish it behind a visible dry.
whenToFish: All summer, and especially good on bright hot days when nothing is hatching. Excellent on tree-lined small streams.
tips: Sitting flush is the whole trick — do not add hackle that lifts it up.
A peacock herl underbody adds the iridescence real beetles have.
When a fish refuses everything on a hot afternoon, try a #16 beetle.
materials: Shell: black foam pulled over the top

name: March Brown
cardText: Traditional mayfly imitation. Important spring hatch, especially in Eastern and Midwestern streams.
imitates: Drowned and emerging March Brown mayflies
summary: A traditional winged wet fly for early spring, when the first big mayflies come off cold water.
body: The March Brown is one of the first substantial mayflies of the year, hatching in early spring when water is still cold and fish are not yet looking hard at the surface. That makes the wet fly version more useful than the dry on many days: trout are feeding, but a foot down rather than on top.

The traditional dressing — a hare's ear body, a mottled brown partridge or hen hackle and a paired quill wing — is a classic example of the old winged wet fly, a style largely displaced by nymphs and now enjoying a quiet revival. Fished on the swing it presents a drowned or emerging insect at exactly the depth cold-water fish want it.

Early season fishing rewards covering water rather than waiting for rises, and a team of wets swung through likely runs is one of the more efficient ways to do that. On a cold April afternoon it will often outfish an indicator rig, and it is considerably more enjoyable.
howToFish: Down and across on a swing, allowing the flies to hang at the end before recasting. Fish it as the point or middle fly on a team of two or three wets.
whenToFish: Early spring during March Brown emergences, and generally through the first weeks of the season when water is cold.
tips: Cover water rather than waiting for rises in early season.
Let the flies hang for several seconds at the end of the swing.
A team of three wets covers three depths at once.

name: Pale Morning Dun
cardText: Premier summer mayfly, especially in the West. Yellowish body and reliable daytime hatch.
imitates: Ephemerella mayfly duns
summary: The defining western summer hatch — a pale yellow mayfly that brings big trout up in the best hours of the day.
body: If the Blue Winged Olive is the hatch of bad weather, the Pale Morning Dun is the hatch of good. Through summer on western rivers, PMDs come off in the late morning and early afternoon in numbers heavy enough to get every fish in a run looking up, and they do it in pleasant conditions on beautiful water. It is, for a lot of anglers, the best fishing of the year.

The colour is genuinely distinctive — a soft pale yellow with an olive or pinkish cast depending on the river — and unlike with the Adams, colour here does matter. Fish see a great many of these insects over several weeks and get educated. Matching the specific shade on your water is worth the trouble.

The other thing worth knowing is that PMD hatches produce famously difficult cripples and stuck-in-the-shuck emergers. When fish are refusing a well-drifted dun during a heavy PMD hatch, they are usually eating something that never fully made it out. A crippled or emerger pattern solves more PMD refusals than any change of tippet.
howToFish: Dead drift to individual working fish rather than fishing the water. Watch the rise form: a clean nose means duns, a bulge or a dorsal fin means emergers just under the film.
whenToFish: Late morning to mid-afternoon through summer, roughly June to August depending on elevation and latitude. Spinner falls in the evening can be even better than the hatch.
tips: Match the shade of yellow on your particular river — it varies more than you would expect.
Keep a cripple pattern in the same size; it answers most refusals.
Fish the spinner fall at dusk. It is quieter, and often bigger fish.
materials: Wing: light dun poly yarn or hackle tips

name: Blue Wing Olive
cardText: Classic hatch-matcher. Essential in U.S. streams.
imitates: Baetis mayfly duns
summary: The small olive mayfly that hatches when the weather is worst — and brings the biggest fish in the river to the surface.
body: Baetis mayflies are the great contrarians of the insect world. They hatch heaviest on cold, grey, drizzling days when every sensible angler has gone home, and they hatch twice a year, in spring and again in autumn. A Blue Winged Olive hatch on a miserable November afternoon will put fish on the surface that you would never otherwise see feeding.

The reason is the weather itself. A newly emerged dun needs time for its wings to dry before it can fly, and on a cold damp day that can take a minute or more. The insect rides the current, helpless and conspicuous, and trout that normally hold deep move up into feeding lanes because the opportunity is genuinely worth it.

The practical challenge is size. These are small insects, commonly #18 to #22, and anglers routinely fish them two sizes too big. If fish are rising steadily and refusing, the problem is almost always size or drag, in that order — not colour, and not pattern.
howToFish: Fine tippet, long leader, and an obsessive dead drift. Position yourself so the fly reaches the fish before the leader does. On flat water, downstream presentations with a reach cast outfish upstream casts by a wide margin.
whenToFish: Spring and autumn, and through winter on tailwaters. Best on overcast, cold, drizzling days — the worse the weather feels, the better the hatch.
tips: Go down to 6X and be honest about whether your drift is really drag-free.
Carry the emerger and the spinner as well as the dun; fish often key on one stage.
A cloudy day in October is worth two bright ones.
materials: Tail: dun hackle fibres or Microfibbets
Wing: dun hackle tips or CDC
searchTerms: what does a blue winged olive imitate

name: Rusty Spinner
cardText: Imitates spent mayflies (often rusty-brown after mating); deadly during spinner falls.
imitates: Spent mayfly spinners lying flat on the surface
summary: The final act of a mayfly's life — wings flat, body spent, drifting dead in the film. Quiet fishing, often the day's best.
body: A mayfly's last act is to mate above the water and fall onto it, wings splayed flat, and die. This happens most evenings through the hatch season, usually in the last hour of light, and it produces some of the most consistent and least crowded fishing of the day. Most anglers have gone to dinner by then.

Spinners lie absolutely flush and absolutely still. There is no wing upright, no hackle, no movement — just a thin rusty body and two transparent wings splayed sideways in the film. That is why hackled patterns fail during a spinner fall and why the imitation is so minimal: anything more is wrong.

The hard part is seeing it. A spent spinner is invisible at any real distance in fading light, and the rises are the softest of the day — a small dimple with no sound. Fish close, fish to specific rises, and accept that you will be setting the hook on faith more than once.
howToFish: Dead drift, no exceptions. Fish to individual rise rings in the last light. Because you often cannot see the fly, set gently on any rise within a foot of where you think it is.
whenToFish: Evenings through the mayfly season, typically the last hour before dark. Also early morning after a heavy overnight fall.
tips: Rusty brown covers a remarkable share of spinner falls.
Grease the leader to within six inches of the fly and leave the fly ungreased.
The rises are dimples, not splashes. Slow your hookset down.
materials: Body: rusty brown dubbing, very sparse
Wing: white or clear poly yarn, tied spent and flat

name: Split Case PMD
cardText: Imitates emerging Pale Morning Dun; split wingcase shows nymph shedding shuck.
imitates: Pale Morning Duns caught in the act of emerging
summary: Mike Mercer's emerger with a split black wingcase that shows the dun breaking out of its shuck. Precise, and unusually convincing.
body: Most emerger patterns suggest a stage; the Split Case shows a moment. A dark, glossy wingcase is tied so it splits open along the top, revealing pale fibres pushing out beneath — exactly what happens as a Pale Morning Dun tears its nymphal skin and starts to climb out. It is one of the more literal imitations in a fly box, and it works.

During a PMD hatch, a large share of the insects are stuck in this state, hanging half-out and going nowhere. Trout learn quickly that these cannot escape, and they will often eat nothing else while the hatch is on. Anglers fishing a clean dun into that situation get refused all afternoon.
It is fished just under or in the film rather than deep. That is the zone where the naturals are trapped, and being a few inches too low is enough to be ignored.
howToFish: Fish it in or just under the surface film, dead drift, on fine tippet. Trailing it eighteen inches behind a visible dry solves the problem of tracking it.
whenToFish: Summer PMD hatches, especially mid-hatch when fish stop taking clean duns but keep working.
tips: If fish are bulging rather than nosing, this is the fly.
Grease the leader, not the fly.

Baetis nymphs swim up, hang in the film and struggle out of their shucks, and the ones that fail drift for a long way in plain view. Trout that appear to be rising to duns are frequently taking emergers an inch below them.

This is the single most common reason anglers get refused during a BWO hatch. The drift is fine, the size is right, the fly is a good imitation of a dun — and the fish are simply eating something else. Switching to an emerger usually resolves it immediately.

The tell is in the rise form. A clean nose and a visible mouth means duns; a humped back, a dorsal fin, or a bulge with no nose showing means the fish is feeding just under the surface and never breaking it.

name: Green Drake

The hatch is short, localised and famously unreliable, which is exactly why it has a reputation. On a good year, in the right week, on the right river, it produces the largest trout of the season on a dry fly. On a bad year it is over before you hear about it.

Because the insect is so large, fish get a good look, and drake refusals are common and maddening. Long leaders, a genuinely drag-free drift, and a fly that sits low rather than perching on hackle points all help. Many anglers do better on a drake emerger than on the dun.

name: Scud
cardText: Effective stillwater pattern. Fishes year-round, near bottom or around weed beds.

summary: A curved, segmented crustacean pattern that is the staple food on most tailwaters and spring creeks.
body: Scuds are small freshwater crustaceans that live in weed beds and gravel in cold, mineral-rich water. On tailwaters and spring creeks they exist in extraordinary densities, and trout in those systems eat them constantly and grow fat doing it. Where scuds are abundant, they are often the single largest component of a trout's diet.

The imitation is straightforward: a curved hook, a translucent dubbed body picked out for legs, and a shellback with a fine wire rib for segmentation. The curve matters — a scud at rest curls, and although a swimming scud actually straightens out, the curved silhouette has caught fish for decades and there is little reason to argue with it.

Colour is worth paying attention to. Live scuds are usually olive, grey or tan; dead and dying ones turn distinctly orange or pink, and trout key on that. An orange scud after a sudden flow change or in the winter can be dramatically more effective than a natural colour.
howToFish: Dead drift near the bottom, ideally along weed bed edges and drop-offs. Small twitches during the drift imitate the erratic swimming motion and often draw the take.
whenToFish: Year round on tailwaters and spring creeks. Especially good in winter, and immediately after a change in flow when scuds get dislodged.
tips: Carry orange and pink as well as olive — dying scuds are a real trigger.
Fish it tight to weed edges rather than in open water.
Pick out the dubbing generously; the legs are what sells it.

name: Elk Hair Caddis
cardText: Al Troth, 1957. Classic high-floating, durable caddis imitation. Great in fast water.

summary: A buoyant, tent-winged caddis imitation that floats through heavy water and takes abuse all day.
body: Caddisflies do not sit politely on the water the way mayflies do. They skitter, they flutter, they run across the surface, and trout chase them with a violence that mayfly rises never have. The Elk Hair Caddis is built for that world: a stiff palmered hackle through the body and a solid wing of hollow elk hair make it one of the most genuinely buoyant dry flies you can tie.

That buoyancy is the reason it has outlasted most of its competition. It rides broken pocket water and fast riffles where a delicate mayfly imitation drowns on the second cast, and it holds up a dropper nymph without going under. On many freestone rivers in summer, an Elk Hair Caddis with a small beadhead hanging eighteen inches below is the entire day's fishing.

It also earns eats when nothing is hatching. The silhouette is close enough to a stonefly, a small hopper, or a moth blown off the bank that fish in fast water rarely take the time to argue. Fish it as a searching pattern on unfamiliar water and you will find out quickly where the players are.
howToFish: Dead drift through riffles and seams, then let it swing and skate at the end. A deliberate twitch just as it starts to drag imitates an adult caddis running for the bank and will move fish that ignored a clean drift.
whenToFish: Late spring through autumn, strongest in evening when caddis are egg-laying. A reliable searching fly on freestone water any time between hatches.
tips: Trim the hackle flat underneath to sit it lower when fish get picky.
Use it as the dry in a dry-dropper rig — few dries hold a bead better.
Tan and olive cover most situations; carry a black one for evening.

name: Royal Wulff
cardText: Lee Wulff's attractor. Bright and visible, great for fast water.

It is a banded peacock body with a bright red floss belt and two white wings, and no entomologist has ever found its equal in a stream sample. It also catches an enormous number of trout, which is a useful reminder that matching the hatch is a tactic rather than a religion.

What it does have is contrast, buoyancy and visibility. The peacock herl has a natural iridescence that reads as something alive; the red band gives a trigger point; the white calf hair wings let you follow the fly through fast water at forty feet. On tumbling freestone streams and in cutthroat country, fish get a fraction of a second to decide, and a fly that looks generally edible and definitely visible wins that argument.

It is at its best where fish are opportunistic rather than educated — small mountain streams, high-country cutthroat water, and pocket water on big freestone rivers. On a heavily fished spring creek it will get looked at and refused. Know which river you are on.
howToFish: Cast it into the fast, broken, awkward water most people walk past. Pocket water, plunge pools, seams behind boulders. Short casts, high rod, and keep it drifting cleanly for the two feet that matter.
whenToFish: Summer on freestone and mountain streams, especially when nothing is hatching and you want to cover water quickly.

name: Stimulator

body: The Stimulator is the workhorse of western summer dry fly fishing. It is large enough to be worth a trout's attention, buoyant enough to ride heavy pocket water and to suspend a weighted nymph beneath it, and visible enough that you can actually fish it in glare and fading light. Very few flies do all three jobs at once.

Its imprecision is deliberate. In orange it reads as a salmonfly or golden stone; in yellow as a big caddis or a small hopper; in olive as almost anything terrestrial that has fallen in. On rough freestone water, where a trout has a moment to decide before the food is gone, that generality is worth more than exact imitation.

This is also the fly that makes dry-dropper fishing practical. A #10 Stimulator will hold a beadhead nymph on eighteen inches of tippet without drowning, which means you are effectively fishing two depths at once while still getting the pleasure of watching a dry fly disappear.

name: Humpy
cardText: Extra-buoyant and versatile attractor. Stays visible and afloat in fast, broken water.

summary: A deer hair humpback attractor that floats like a cork through water where nothing else stays up.

In whitewater, plunge pools and boiling pocket water where a conventional dry is drowned within two drifts, a Humpy is still up and visible.

It imitates nothing in particular and reads as everything in general — a stonefly, a big caddis, a beetle blown in from the bank. Fast-water trout make quick decisions on limited information, and a chunky buoyant silhouette drifting overhead is enough information.

It is a genuinely difficult fly to tie well, which is why fewer people fish it than should. In high-country cutthroat streams and steep freestone creeks it remains one of the most effective dry flies available.

name: Madam X
cardText: Hopper/stonefly attractor. Foam, rubber legs. Western classic.

It reads as a hopper, a stonefly, or a large generic terrestrial depending on colour and size, and fast-water trout rarely take the time to distinguish.

It is also an excellent dry-dropper anchor, which is how most people now fish it. A yellow Madam X in #10 with a beadhead eighteen inches below covers a summer freestone river about as efficiently as any rig there is.

That is the whole idea, and it is a good demonstration of how narrow the gap between an imitative fly and an attractor can be. Everything about the silhouette, size and posture stays imitative; only the colour goes strange.

Purple appears to work as a trigger in a way that is not fully explained. One plausible reading is that against a bright sky, a purple body produces a darker, more defined silhouette than grey does, giving a fish a clearer target. Whatever the mechanism, on Montana and Idaho rivers it has become a genuine confidence pattern for a lot of guides.

It is most useful in the middle of a hatch when fish have started refusing conventional imitations, and as a searching dry when nothing is coming off at all. Because the profile is a proper parachute mayfly, it does not carry the penalty that a loud attractor usually does on selective fish.

name: Griffith's Gnat
cardText: By George Griffith, Michigan, late 1930s. Great cluster midge pattern.

summary: Peacock herl palmered with grizzly hackle — a tiny scruffy fly that reads as a knot of mating midges.
body: Midges hatch every month of the year, which makes them the most reliably available trout food there is and the reason winter fishing is possible at all. Individually they are almost too small to imitate. But midges mate in clusters on the surface, several insects tangled together into a single drifting mass, and that cluster is a target a trout will move for.

The Griffith's Gnat is that cluster. Peacock herl gives the dark, iridescent mass; the grizzly hackle palmered over it gives the impression of many legs and wings at once without resolving into any single insect. Squint at one on the water and it looks like a small piece of dark chaos, which is exactly right.

It is a fly that rewards patience over distance. Midging fish rise quietly and repeatedly in slow water, often in the same lane, and they are not going far to eat. Find one, watch it for a minute to learn its rhythm, and put the fly where it is going to be.

name: Trico
cardText: Tiny mayfly for summer hatches. Demands precision.

summary: A mayfly small enough to test your eyesight and your patience — and a morning hatch so dense trout feed in a trance.
body: Tricos hatch in extraordinary numbers on late summer mornings, mate in clouds above the water, and fall spent onto the surface in a carpet. The result is one of the most reliable and most difficult forms of dry fly fishing there is: dozens of visibly feeding trout, eating steadily, in a food supply so dense that your single artificial is competing with thousands of naturals.

The flies themselves are tiny — #22 to #26 is normal — with black bodies and pale wings. At that size, tippet diameter and drift quality matter more than pattern. Most Trico failures are drag failures that the angler cannot see.

The compensation is timing. The spinner fall happens at roughly the same time every morning through the hatch, often within a half hour, so once you have worked out the schedule on your river you can arrive, fish the peak, and be finished by mid-morning.
howToFish: Fish to individual rising fish on 6X or 7X. Cast slightly downstream with a reach so the fly arrives before the leader. Accept that you will refuse more than you hook.
whenToFish: Late summer and early autumn mornings, typically from soon after dawn until mid-morning.
tips: Note the time of the spinner fall — it repeats within a half hour daily.

name: Royal Coachman
cardText: Classic attractor (1878 origin); peacock/red floss body. Many variants exist.

summary: Peacock, red floss and white wings. The most famous American fly that imitates absolutely nothing.
body: The Royal Coachman is the fly that taught American anglers that imitation is optional. It descends from the older English Coachman, to which someone added a band of red silk, and the result is a fly of such obvious artificiality that its continued success is slightly embarrassing to anyone who takes matching the hatch seriously.

It catches fish because it combines three strong triggers: the iridescence of peacock herl, a sharp band of contrasting colour, and bright white wings that a trout can locate instantly. On small streams and in wild-fish country where trout must eat opportunistically or go hungry, those triggers are enough. Curiosity and competition do the rest.

It also occupies a genuine place in the history of the sport — for decades in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it was probably the best-known trout fly in America, tied as a dry, a wet and a streamer. Fishing one on a small brook trout stream is a pleasantly direct connection to that period.
howToFish: Fish it as a searching dry on small streams and pocket water — short casts, quick drifts, cover a lot of water. Also fishes well as a wet fly on the swing.
whenToFish: Summer on small streams and high-country water, particularly for wild brook trout and cutthroat that see few anglers.
tips: Best where fish are opportunistic rather than educated.

name: Pink Albert
cardText: Imitates Pink Albert mayfly (Epeorus albertae); effective Western PMD variant.

summary: A pale mayfly with a distinctly pink cast, and a western evening hatch that anglers reliably fish the wrong colour for.

It is often lumped in with the Pale Morning Duns hatching around the same time, which is exactly the mistake that gets anglers refused: the sizes are similar, the timing overlaps, and the colour is not the same.

It matters because these hatches can be dense and the fish get a long look. When trout are working steadily during a summer evening and a good PMD imitation is being ignored, the pink body is very often the missing variable.

It hatches in the warmer parts of the day and into the evening, and like most Epeorus species the emergence happens close to the riverbed, with duns arriving at the surface already able to fly. That makes the surface window short and the emerger stage disproportionately important.
howToFish: Dead drift to working fish on fine tippet. Because the duns leave the surface quickly, an emerger fished in the film often outproduces the dun.
whenToFish: Summer, particularly evenings, on western freestone rivers.
tips: If a PMD imitation is being refused during a summer evening, try the pink.

Match the tint, not just the size.
