name: Adams
cardText: Created in Michigan, 1922. Most famous dry. Imitates mayflies broadly.
imitates: Adult mayflies and midges, generically
summary: The most useful dry fly ever tied — a grey, buggy silhouette that passes for almost any mayfly on the water.
body: The Adams is the fly you tie on when you can see rises but cannot see what is causing them. Its grizzly-and-brown mixed hackle reads as mottled rather than any one colour, and the muted grey body sits in the middle of the range covered by most mayfly duns. That vagueness is the whole point. A trout looking up through moving water is reading size, silhouette and posture far more than it is reading colour, and the Adams gets all three approximately right for an enormous number of insects.

It has survived a century of fly design because it fails gracefully. A pattern tied to imitate one specific insect is superb during that hatch and nearly useless outside it. The Adams is rarely the single best fly on the water and almost never the wrong one. If you carry a box to an unfamiliar river, this is the pattern that keeps you fishing while you work out what is actually going on.

Size matters more than anything else with this fly. The same dressing in #12 suggests a big spring mayfly; in #20 it reads as a midge cluster or a tiny olive. Most anglers carry it far too large. When fish are refusing, drop two sizes before you change patterns.
howToFish: Dead drift on a fine tippet, upstream or across, with enough slack that the fly moves at exactly the speed of the current. Any drag at all and a good fish will refuse it. Cast to the rise ring rather than to the fish, and give it a foot or two of lead.
whenToFish: Any time you see mayfly duns on the surface, and any time you see rises you cannot identify. Strongest from the first spring hatches through autumn, and effective through winter in smaller sizes on tailwaters.
tips: Carry it in #14, #16 and #18 before you carry any other dry fly.
When fish refuse a standard Adams, switch to the parachute version — the lower profile often solves it.

name: Egg
cardText: Effective during/after spawns; imitates trout/salmon eggs drifting freely.
imitates: Loose fish eggs drifting downstream from a spawning bed
summary: A ball of bright yarn imitating a loose fish egg — the highest-calorie, lowest-effort meal in the river.
body: When fish spawn, a significant proportion of the eggs never make it into the gravel. They wash loose and drift downstream, and every trout below the redd knows it. An egg is pure protein and fat requiring no pursuit whatsoever, and during a spawning run trout will position themselves specifically to intercept them and eat little else.

The imitation is a ball of bright yarn — chartreuse, peach, orange, pink — trimmed round. Colour matters more than you would expect: fresh eggs are brighter and more translucent, older ones go pale and opaque, and matching what is actually drifting can make a real difference on a pressured river.

It carries an ethical obligation. Fishing eggs below spawning fish is legitimate; wading through active redds to do it is not. Learn to recognise a redd — a clean, pale patch of disturbed gravel — and stay off it. Fish the water below, and leave spawning fish alone.
howToFish: Dead drift deep under an indicator, in the water below spawning gravel. No action, no strip — an egg simply tumbles with the current.
whenToFish: Autumn through spring, during and immediately after salmon and trout spawning runs.
tips: Never wade through a redd. Fish the run below it.
Match the shade of the naturals — fresh eggs are brighter than old ones.
Trail a small nymph eighteen inches behind it.

name: San Juan Worm
cardText: Controversial but effective. Simple chenille worm, deadly after rainstorms.
imitates: Aquatic worms
summary: A piece of red chenille that catches trout everywhere and starts arguments in every fly shop in America.
body: The San Juan Worm is a short length of red or pink chenille on a hook, and it is the most divisive fly in the sport. Purists dismiss it as bait with a hook in it. Everyone who has fished the San Juan, the Bighorn, or any tailwater in high water knows perfectly well that it works, and works when almost nothing else does.

It is not a trick. Aquatic worms genuinely live in silt and gravel in enormous numbers, and every time flows rise or the riverbed is disturbed they get washed into the drift. Trout eat them eagerly because they are large, soft and defenceless. A drifting red worm is a real and frequent event in a trout's life, not an insult to its intelligence.

Its finest hour is high, off-coloured water — spring runoff, a dam release, or the day after heavy rain, when clarity is poor and the fish need something substantial and visible. Under those conditions it is not merely effective; it is often the correct answer.
howToFish: Dead drift deep under an indicator, usually as the top fly with something smaller trailing. Get it right down on the bottom — worms do not swim.
whenToFish: Year round, and at its very best in high, coloured or rising water after rain or a flow change.
tips: Red, pink and wine all have their days; carry more than one.
The day after heavy rain is San Juan Worm weather.
Fish it deep. If it is not near the bottom, it is not doing its job.

Body: red, pink or wine ultra chenille, singed at both ends

name: Bass Popper
cardText: Imitates injured baitfish, frogs, or large insects skittering on the surface.
imitates: Injured baitfish, frogs and large insects struggling on the surface
summary: A hard-faced surface popper that chugs, spits and gets eaten with real violence. The most entertaining fly in the deck.
body: A popper does not imitate anything at rest. Its entire function is the noise and the disturbance it makes when you pull it — a pop, a spray of water, a spreading ring — which reads to a predatory fish as something wounded and worth attacking. Bass in particular respond to it with a ferocity that trout fishing rarely offers.

The face is the working part. A flat or cupped front pushes water and makes the sound; a more pointed face slides and gurgles instead. Both have their days, and the retrieve matters at least as much as the fly: hard pops for aggressive fish, small gurgles and long pauses when they are being cautious.

The pause is where most fish are actually caught. A popper sitting motionless in the rings of its own disturbance is at its most convincing, and the strike usually comes just as you have decided nothing is there.
howToFish: Cast to structure — lily pads, timber, undercut banks — let the rings settle, then pop it once and wait. Vary the rhythm until fish tell you what they want. Strike on feel, not on sight.
whenToFish: Late spring through early autumn, best in warm water at dawn and dusk.
tips: The pause sells it. Wait longer than feels natural.
Strike when you feel weight — striking at the splash pulls it away.
Use a short, stout leader; poppers are air-resistant and hard to turn over.
materials: Body: cork, balsa or hard foam with a cupped face
